title: The Book of the Twelve
lead: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi are called the Minor Prophets because they are short. The Hebrew Bible counts them as one scroll, "the Twelve", and the question of whether they were also written and edited as one book is debated.

sections.b: Sirach 49:10 praises "the twelve prophets" as a group, the Talmud says the small prophets were written together so they would not be lost (Bava Batra 13b-14b) and gives their writing to the Men of the Great Assembly (15a), and Josephus's count of twenty-two books in Against Apion is usually read as counting the Twelve as one.

The manuscripts support the one-scroll view. Judean desert copies of the Twelve are the Hebrew scroll from Wadi Murabba'at (MurXII), the Qumran scrolls 4QXIIa to 4QXIIg, and a Greek scroll of the Twelve from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr). The Qumran scrolls are published in DJD 15 and the Greek scroll in DJD 8. For Hosea, 4QXIIc (4Q78), 4QXIId (4Q79) and 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserve parts of the book.

The Masoretic Text runs Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. The Greek runs Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum and then as the Hebrew. Each order creates different neighbors and links.

Joel 3:16 and Amos 1:2 share their words, as do Joel 3:18 and Amos 9:13; Amos 9:12 ends with Edom and Obadiah is about Edom; Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2 repeat the creed of Exodus 34:6. Nogalski, Schart and Sweeney read the Twelve as edited into a unit; Ben Zvi and Barton doubt a single book. Readers should treat the unity of the Twelve as a debated view.
